name: Integral point sets in general position (no three collinear, no four concyclic)
description: construct() -> {'D': D, 'points': [[[x_num, x_den], [y_num, y_den]], ...]} describing 3 to 12 distinct points (x, y*sqrt(D)) with rational x, y (|numerators|, denominators <= 10^40) and squarefree D <= 10^12. All pairwise distances must be rational (equivalently integral after scaling), no three points collinear and no four concyclic, all checked with exact rational arithmetic. Maximize the number of points. A valid set certifies such configurations of that size; 8 points would be new.

sources.locator: Tobias Kreisel and Sascha Kurz, There Are Integral Heptagons, no Three Points on a Line, no Four on a Circle (2008). Crossref record inspected; Erdős Problem #213 page inspected: Anning and Erdős excluded infinite sets, Harborth found 5 points, Kreisel and Kurz 7 points (the best construction), and 8 points remain open. Every planar integral point set has a characteristic D putting its points at (a, b*sqrt(D)) after a similarity (Kemnitz), so the representation is general. A valid set certifies such configurations of that size; 8 points would be new.
Erdős Problem #213 (open); statement, history and current bounds reviewed 2026-09-24.

name: Point sets without an empty convex hexagon (rediscovering 29 points)
description: construct() -> list of 1..30 distinct integer points [x, y] with |x|, |y| <= 10^6 and no three collinear. No six points may form a convex hexagon with no other point inside (exact search over all convex chains anchored at their lowest vertex). Maximize the number of points; the optimum is 29. name: Twelve rational points with many three-point lines (orchard problem)
description: construct() -> exactly 12 distinct integer points [x, y] with |x|, |y| <= 10^30 (any rational configuration can be scaled to integers). Maximize the number of lines containing exactly three of the points, computed exactly; the optimum is 19. The real maximum for 12 points is 19, and the group law on a rational cubic with 12-torsion realizes it with rational points, so the rational optimum is also 19.

sources.locator: Ben Green and Terence Tao, On Sets Defining Few Ordinary Lines (2013). Crossref records inspected (Green-Tao 2013; Burr-Grünbaum-Sloane 1974); OEIS A003035 inspected: maximal numbers of 3-point lines for n <= 14 with a(12) = 19, a(15) in {31, 32}; Erdős Problem #669 page inspected. A local test builds 12 rational torsion points of an elliptic curve with a 12-torsion point, which realize 19 lines. The real maximum for 12 points is 19, and the group law on a rational cubic with 12-torsion realizes it with rational points, so the rational optimum is also 19.
Erdős Problem #669 (open); statement, history and current bounds reviewed 2026-09-24.

name: Contact numbers of 32 unit pennies on the triangular lattice
description: construct() -> exactly 32 distinct integer pairs [a, b] with |a|, |b| <= 64 denoting lattice points a + b*omega, omega = exp(i*pi/3), which are at mutual distance at least one. Maximize the number of pairs at distance exactly one; Harborth's theorem gives the optimum floor(3n - sqrt(12n - 3)) = 76. Harborth's formula gives 76 for n = 32 and triangular-lattice spirals attain it, so the lattice restriction loses nothing.

name: Eight planar points maximizing the product of distances at fixed diameter
description: construct() -> 8 distinct points [x, y] (floats, |coordinate| < 10^6). The score is Delta/n^n, where Delta is the product over ordered pairs of distances after scaling the set to diameter 2; the regular octagon scores exactly 1. Maximize. Scores above 1 beat the regular octagon; the paper's constructions show this is possible, but no value for n = 8 is recorded here.

name: Sixteen frequencies whose cosine sum stays shallow (Chowla's cosine problem)
description: construct() -> 16 distinct integers in 1..200. The score is min over theta of sum cos(a*theta), divided by sqrt(16), computed by dense sampling of the full circle and golden-section refinement of the deepest local minima (accuracy about 1e-9). Maximize (make the minimum as shallow as possible). Shallow minima for 16 frequencies probe the finite side of Chowla's problem; no finite optimum is documented.

name: Flattest plus-minus-one polynomials with 24 coefficients (minimum sup norm)
description: construct() -> 24 coefficients in {+1, -1} of P(z) = sum c_k z^k. The score is max over |z| = 1 of |P(z)| divided by sqrt(24), computed by dense sampling and golden-section refinement of the highest peaks (accuracy about 1e-9). Minimize; the exhaustive optimum is 1.2583758. The exact minimum for 24 coefficients (degree 23) is recovered; Odlyzko's online tables list the optimal polynomials.
